Front. Environ. Sci., 28 October 2026

Sec. Environmental Economics and Management

Volume 14 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1908807

Digital transformation and corporate ESG performance: green technological innovation, market concentration, and the twin transformation perspective

  • FW

    Fang Wang 1,2

  • MF

    Mohd Fahmi Ghazali 1*

  • PH

    Pengfei Hu 2

  • 1. Faculty of Economics and Management (FEP),Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia,UKM, Bangi, Selangor, Malaysia

  • 2. School of Business, Shanxi Technology and Business University, Taiyuan, China

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

This study examines whether, how, and under what market-structure conditions corporate digital transformation improves environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Building on the twin green and digital transformation perspective, this study conceptualizes digital transformation as a dynamic green digital capability rather than merely the adoption of digital technologies. By integrating the Natural Resource-Based View, Stakeholder Theory, and the Porter Hypothesis, we develop a framework in which digital transformation enhances ESG performance by strengthening firms’ data-driven sustainability capabilities and enabling green technological innovation. Using panel data from Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2023, we find that digital transformation is positively associated with ESG performance, measured by Huazheng ESG ratings. Green technological innovation mediates this relationship, and the empirical results indicate that the mediation is partial and economically modest, suggesting that green innovation is only one mechanism within a broader set of digitalization–ESG channels. Market concentration strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, indicating that firms in more concentrated industries are better able to appropriate returns from long-term digital and sustainability investments. Additional heterogeneity analyses show that the positive effect of digital transformation is observed across regions and ownership types. In pollution-related industry subsamples, the effect is significant among non-high-polluting firms but not statistically significant among high-polluting firms; however, the between-group difference is not statistically significant. This study contributes to the literature by clarifying the innovation mechanism and market-structure boundary condition through which digital transformation supports comprehensive ESG improvement. The findings suggest that the ESG value of digital transformation depends not only on whether firms adopt digital technologies, but also on whether they develop dynamic green digital capabilities and operate in market environments that support long-term sustainability investment.

1 Introduction

Climate change and the transition toward sustainable development have become central challenges for firms, regulators, and capital markets. In response to increasing environmental pressure, China has committed to peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060. These national targets have accelerated the need for firms to improve environmental governance, resource efficiency, information disclosure, and broader environmental, social, and governance performance (Lee et al., 2023). At the same time, digital technologies such as big data analytics, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and the Internet of Things are reshaping corporate operations, resource allocation, and strategic decision-making (Liu et al., 2022). These developments raise an important question: whether and how corporate digital transformation enables firms to convert digital capabilities into improved ESG performance (Chen et al., 2023).

This question matters to multiple groups of stakeholders. For corporate managers, digital transformation requires substantial investment in data infrastructure, organizational restructuring, digital talent, and process redesign, but its sustainability value remains uncertain. For investors, ESG ratings have become increasingly important signals for evaluating firms’ long-term risk, legitimacy, and responsible investment potential. For regulators, digital technologies provide new tools for environmental monitoring, information disclosure, and corporate governance supervision. For customers, suppliers, employees, and local communities, firms’ digital capabilities may affect transparency, environmental responsibility, labor protection, product safety, and broader stakeholder responsiveness. Therefore, understanding whether digital transformation improves ESG performance is not only a technical issue, but also a strategic, governance, and public-policy issue.

China provides an appropriate and theoretically meaningful context for examining this issue. First, China is simultaneously undergoing digital upgrading and green transition. National strategies related to the digital economy, industrial Internet development, smart manufacturing, carbon peaking, and carbon neutrality have encouraged firms to integrate digital technologies into production, governance, disclosure, and environmental management. This simultaneous pressure for digitalization and sustainability makes China a suitable setting for studying twin green and digital transformation.

Second, Chinese A-share listed firms display substantial variation in digital transformation, ESG performance, green technological innovation, ownership structure, regional development, industry pollution intensity, and market concentration. This variation allows us to examine not only whether digital transformation improves ESG performance, but also how this relationship operates through green technological innovation and when it becomes stronger or weaker under different market-structure conditions.

Third, although China has distinctive institutional characteristics, it is representative of large emerging economies where firms face simultaneous pressures from environmental regulation, digital-economy development, investor attention, and stakeholder legitimacy demands. Therefore, evidence from China can enrich understanding of how firms in transition economies convert dynamic digital capabilities into sustainability outcomes. At the same time, the Chinese setting should be interpreted as analytically representative rather than universally generalizable: it offers a theoretically rich context for studying large emerging economies undergoing simultaneous digital upgrading, environmental regulation, and ESG institutionalization, while cross-country validation remains an important direction for future research.

Digital transformation has increasingly become a strategic priority for firms seeking to improve operational efficiency, organizational adaptability, and sustainability governance. It can fundamentally change production processes and organizational arrangements by streamlining workflows and improving productivity. As an enabling capability, digital transformation can support green technological innovation by reducing information-processing costs, improving coordination efficiency, and facilitating resource allocation for risky and long-term innovation activities (Kraus et al., 2021). From the perspective of the Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV), digital technologies can be understood as strategic resources that help companies develop pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development competencies (Hart, 1995; Hart and Dowell, 2011). Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies directly support green innovations as they help optimize research and development (R&D) and production processes. In addition, the market-oriented allocation of data as a production factor may further promote green innovation by reducing information asymmetry and easing financing constraints (Wang et al., 2025; Wang H. et al., 2023).

At a broader level, digital transformation is reshaping market competition and industry ecosystems. Competition is increasingly shifting from traditional price- and scale-based competition toward data-driven, platform-based, and sustainability-oriented competition. In this context, green technological innovation is not merely a compliance response to environmental regulation; rather, it can become a strategic mechanism through which firms develop differentiated competitive advantages. This logic is consistent with the Porter Hypothesis, which emphasizes that environmental pressure may stimulate innovation and generate compensation effects (Ziaei and Roshani, 2024). In this changed market context, green technological innovation should not be viewed merely as a compliance cost associated with environmental regulation. Instead, consistent with the Porter Hypothesis, it can serve as a strategic mechanism through which firms improve resource efficiency, reduce compliance costs, and create differentiated competitive advantages through innovation compensation effects (Ambec and Barla, 2002; Hart, 1995).

Recent studies have begun to examine the relationships among digital transformation, green innovation, ESG performance, and market competition (Asif et al., 2023; Li and Rasiah, 2024; Ren et al., 2024; Su, 2025; Sun et al., 2026). For instance, prior work has explored how digital transformation affects ESG performance through green innovation and internal control, how market competition shapes digitalization–ESG relationships, and how ESG–digital synergies influence corporate decarbonization. These studies provide valuable insights, but they have not fully developed an integrated framework that links dynamic green digital capabilities, green technological innovation, comprehensive ESG performance, and market-structure conditions.

Existing research has provided important evidence that digital transformation can improve ESG performance, green innovation, environmental disclosure, and corporate sustainability. However, three important gaps remain.

First, prior studies often treat digital transformation mainly as the adoption or disclosure of digital technologies, while paying insufficient attention to its capability-based meaning. From a twin transformation perspective, digital transformation is better understood as a dynamic green digital capability that allows firms to sense sustainability-related information, process environmental and stakeholder data, coordinate internal and external resources, and reconfigure organizational routines for ESG improvement.

Second, the mechanism through which digital transformation improves comprehensive ESG performance remains insufficiently explained. Green technological innovation is often examined as an environmental outcome, but ESG performance is broader than environmental performance. It also includes social responsibility, governance quality, information disclosure, and stakeholder responsiveness. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify why and how an environmental innovation channel can contribute to comprehensive ESG ratings.

Third, the boundary conditions under which digital transformation generates stronger ESG benefits remain underexplored. Market concentration is especially relevant because it may have two competing effects. On the one hand, concentrated markets may reduce competitive pressure and create monopoly complacency. On the other hand, they may provide resource slack, stable cash flows, and stronger appropriability, allowing firms to sustain long-term digital and ESG investments.

To address these gaps, this study is guided by the following research questions:

  • RQ1: Does corporate digital transformation, understood as a dynamic green digital capability rather than mere technology adoption, improve firms’ comprehensive ESG performance?

  • RQ2: Does digital transformation promote green technological innovation, and does green technological innovation subsequently improve ESG performance?

  • RQ3: Does green technological innovation mediate the relationship between digital transformation and corporate ESG performance?

  • RQ4: Does market concentration strengthen or weaken the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance?

  • RQ5: Do the effects of digital transformation on ESG performance vary across regions, ownership types, and pollution-related industry groups?

This study makes three contributions.

First, it contributes to the literature on digital transformation and ESG performance by introducing a twin green and digital transformation perspective. Instead of treating digital transformation as simple technology adoption, this study conceptualizes it as a dynamic green digital capability that enables firms to collect, process, integrate, and apply sustainability-related information for ESG improvement.

Second, it clarifies the innovation-based mechanism linking digital transformation to comprehensive ESG performance. By decomposing the mediation logic into the effect of digital transformation on green technological innovation and the effect of green technological innovation on ESG performance, this study explains how digital capabilities can be translated into sustainability outcomes while acknowledging that green innovation is only one channel among several ESG-enhancing mechanisms.

Third, it identifies market concentration as an important boundary condition. By examining whether market concentration strengthens or weakens the digital transformation–ESG relationship, this study extends the Porter Hypothesis to a market-structure setting and shows that the ESG value of digital transformation depends on firms’ ability to appropriate returns from long-term digital and sustainability investments.

2 Literature review and hypothesis development

2.1 Twin Green and digital transformation

The concept of twin green and digital transformation emphasizes the mutually reinforcing relationship between digitalization and sustainability transformation. Rather than viewing digital transformation and green transformation as two separate strategic agendas, the twin transformation perspective suggests that digital technologies can enable firms to redesign production processes, monitor environmental performance, optimize resource use, improve sustainability disclosure, and develop green technological innovation.

In this study, digital transformation represents the capability side of the twin transformation. It is conceptualized as a dynamic green digital capability through which firms collect, process, integrate, and apply data related to production, energy consumption, emissions, supply chains, governance, disclosure, and stakeholder expectations. Green transformation, by contrast, refers to the sustainability-oriented outcomes of deploying these digital capabilities, including green technological innovation and improved ESG performance.

This perspective helps clarify the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance. Digital transformation does not automatically generate sustainability outcomes. Its ESG value depends on whether firms can embed digital technologies into environmental management, green innovation, governance transparency, stakeholder communication, and organizational routines. Therefore, the twin transformation perspective provides an overarching logic for examining whether digital transformation improves ESG performance, how green technological innovation transmits this effect, and when market concentration strengthens or weakens the relationship.

2.2 Integrated theoretical framework

Building on the twin green and digital transformation perspective, this study integrates the Natural Resource-Based View, Stakeholder Theory, and the Porter Hypothesis to explain how dynamic green digital capabilities are converted into comprehensive corporate ESG performance. Instead of treating these theories as separate explanations, we use them to develop a three-layer theoretical framework that links internal capability formation, external stakeholder pressure, and innovation-based compensation.

First, the Natural Resource-Based View provides the capability foundation of the framework. The NRBV emphasizes that firms can achieve competitive advantage by developing capabilities related to pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development. From this perspective, digital transformation enhances firms’ data-driven environmental management capabilities. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, cloud computing, and industrial Internet platforms enable firms to collect and process environmental information, monitor emissions, optimize energy consumption, improve resource allocation, and coordinate green supply-chain activities. Therefore, digital transformation can provide the internal capability base needed for pollution prevention, resource efficiency, and sustainable product development.

Second, Stakeholder Theory explains why firms are motivated to deploy these digital capabilities for sustainability and ESG-related purposes. Firms operate within a network of stakeholders, including governments, investors, customers, suppliers, employees, communities, and the media. As these stakeholders increasingly demand environmental accountability, firms face growing pressure to disclose environmental information, reduce pollution, and improve environmental responsiveness. Digital transformation enhances information transparency and enables firms to trace, process, and communicate environmental data more effectively. Thus, stakeholder pressure transforms digital capabilities from general operational resources into tools for environmental governance and legitimacy management.

Third, the Porter Hypothesis explains the innovation mechanism through which digital capabilities and stakeholder pressures are translated into environmental improvements and broader ESG outcomes. According to the Porter Hypothesis, environmental pressure may stimulate innovation and generate compensation effects by improving resource efficiency, reducing compliance costs, and creating new competitive advantages. In the context of digital transformation, digital technologies reduce information asymmetry, coordination costs, and technological search costs, thereby facilitating green technological innovation. Green technological innovation then improves corporate ESG performance through cleaner production, energy conservation, emissions reduction, and resource recycling.

Finally, market concentration serves as a boundary condition in this integrated framework. Firms in more concentrated industries often possess greater market power, more stable cash flows, stronger resource slack, and greater strategic discretion. These conditions may allow them to convert digital efficiency gains into long-term environmental investments and green technological innovation. In contrast, firms in highly competitive industries may face stronger short-term cost pressures, limiting their ability to sustain digital and green transformation. Therefore, market concentration may strengthen the positive relationship between digital transformation and corporate ESG performance.

Taken together, the three theories form a sequential and complementary framework. The NRBV explains the capability base created by digital transformation; Stakeholder Theory explains the external pressure and legitimacy motivation that direct these capabilities toward ESG governance; and the Porter Hypothesis explains the innovation-based mechanism through which digital capabilities and stakeholder pressure are converted into ESG improvements. Market concentration further conditions this process by shaping firms’ resource slack, strategic discretion, and ability to appropriate returns from long-term sustainability investments.

2.3 Digital transformation and corporate ESG performance

Corresponding to RQ1, this subsection develops the direct-effect hypothesis linking digital transformation to comprehensive ESG performance. Consistent with the twin transformation perspective, digital transformation is treated as a dynamic green digital capability rather than simply the adoption of digital technologies.

Building on the integrated framework, this subsection develops the direct-effect hypothesis by combining the NRBV and Stakeholder Theory.

The Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV) provides an important theoretical foundation for explaining how digital transformation can enhance corporate ESG performance through improved environmental management capabilities and broader sustainability governance. Hart (1995) argues that the source of competitive advantage is gradually shifting to those organizational capabilities that enable environmentally sustainable economic activities. Based on that premise, Hart and Dowell (2011) identify three strategic capabilities: pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development. Each of these strategies calls for different organizational capabilities, which digital technologies have the power to augment. Prior research generally conceptualizes digital transformation as a multidimensional process involving technology adoption, process reconfiguration, and strategic renewal. Digital transformation, viewed through the lenses of resource-based view and dynamic capability theory, involves more than just the use of digital technologies; it is a strategic endeavor by which companies redefine their resource bases and develop new dynamic capabilities for dealing with environmental changes.

At the core of this process is the use of data as a strategic production factor to reshape enterprise operations, decision-making, and business models through technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and cloud computing (Vial, 2021). Prior research suggests that digital transformation provides an important capability base for green innovation by optimizing resource allocation, improving information-processing efficiency, and enhancing organizational agility (Kraus et al., 2021). Huang and Lau (2024) argue that digital transformation leads to green innovation quality improvement in Chinese enterprises. The effect is made stronger by executives who have digital knowledge and experience. Wang et al. (2024) found that digital transformation improves ESG performance indirectly by increasing total factor productivity. In other words, their findings disclose a path through which digitalization increases overall operational efficiency and thereby freeing resources for sustainability-related investment (Plekhanov et al., 2023).

From the perspective of the Natural Resource-Based View, the ESG value of digital transformation lies in its ability to strengthen firms’ environmentally relevant capabilities. The NRBV argues that competitive advantage can be created through pollution prevention, product stewardship, and sustainable development capabilities. Digital transformation can reinforce these capabilities by enabling real-time environmental monitoring, data-driven resource allocation, energy-efficiency optimization, green supply-chain coordination, and sustainability-oriented process redesign. Therefore, digital transformation should not be treated merely as the adoption of digital technologies, but as a dynamic green digital capability that helps firms reconfigure organizational routines toward sustainability objectives.

Stakeholder Theory further explains why firms deploy digital capabilities for ESG improvement. Firms face increasing demands from governments, investors, customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and media for environmental accountability, social responsibility, governance transparency, and credible disclosure. Digital technologies improve the collection, processing, verification, and communication of ESG-related information, thereby enhancing firms’ ability to respond to stakeholder expectations and maintain organizational legitimacy. In this sense, digital transformation strengthens not only environmental management but also social and governance practices through improved transparency, internal control, risk monitoring, and stakeholder communication.

Combining the capability logic of the NRBV and the legitimacy logic of Stakeholder Theory, digital transformation can improve comprehensive ESG performance through both internal capability-building and external legitimacy-enhancing channels. Firms with stronger dynamic green digital capabilities are more likely to identify ESG risks, allocate resources to sustainability projects, improve disclosure quality, and respond to stakeholder concerns in a timely manner.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H1Digital transformation, conceptualized as a dynamic green digital capability, is positively associated with corporate ESG performance.

2.4 Green technological innovation as an innovation-based mediation mechanism

Corresponding to RQ2 and RQ3, this subsection explains how digital transformation affects green technological innovation, how green technological innovation contributes to ESG performance, and why green technological innovation serves as a mediating mechanism.

The NRBV suggests that firms need to develop specific environmental capabilities to achieve sustainable competitive advantage. Digital transformation provides an important capability base for such environmental capability development. By integrating artificial intelligence, big data analytics, cloud computing, industrial Internet platforms, and Internet of Things technologies into production and R&D processes, firms can identify environmental inefficiencies, monitor energy consumption, analyze emission patterns, search for cleaner technologies, coordinate green R&D resources, and redesign production routines. These functions correspond to the NRBV tenets of pollution prevention and sustainable development.

The Porter Hypothesis provides a complementary innovation-based explanation. It suggests that environmental pressure can stimulate innovation when firms possess the capabilities needed to respond efficiently. Digital transformation reduces information-processing costs, technological-search costs, and coordination costs, thereby increasing firms’ ability to transform environmental and stakeholder pressures into green technological innovation. In addition, digital transformation improves the allocation of innovation resources by helping firms evaluate green R&D projects, identify commercially viable low-carbon technologies, and coordinate cross-functional innovation teams. Therefore, digital transformation is expected to promote green technological innovation.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H2aDigital transformation positively affects green technological innovation.

Green technological innovation contributes to ESG performance through the combined mechanisms proposed by the NRBV, Stakeholder Theory, and the Porter Hypothesis. From the NRBV perspective, green technological innovation enhances pollution prevention, cleaner production, energy conservation, resource recycling, and sustainable product development capabilities. These improvements directly strengthen the environmental dimension of ESG performance by reducing resource consumption, emissions, and environmental risks (Clément et al., 2022).

From the perspective of Stakeholder Theory, green technological innovation also helps firms respond to the expectations of regulators, investors, customers, communities, and other stakeholders. Firms engaging in green innovation are more likely to improve environmental disclosure, demonstrate regulatory compliance, strengthen internal governance procedures, enhance sustainability legitimacy, and build trust with external stakeholders. These actions may be reflected not only in environmental scores but also in social responsibility, governance transparency, and disclosure-related aspects of ESG ratings.

The Porter Hypothesis further suggests that green technological innovation can generate innovation compensation effects by improving resource efficiency, reducing environmental compliance costs, and creating differentiation advantages. Therefore, green technological innovation is expected to improve comprehensive ESG performance.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H2bGreen technological innovation positively affects corporate ESG performance.

Integrating the three theories, green technological innovation can be viewed as an innovation-based pathway through which dynamic green digital capabilities are converted into ESG outcomes. Digital transformation provides the capability foundation emphasized by the NRBV; stakeholder pressure directs these capabilities toward environmental and ESG-related objectives; and the Porter Hypothesis explains how these capabilities and pressures are transformed into green innovation and performance improvement. However, because ESG performance is broader than environmental innovation and also includes social responsibility, governance quality, internal control, disclosure transparency, and stakeholder responsiveness, green technological innovation is expected to serve as an important, but not necessarily exclusive, mediation mechanism through which digital transformation influences ESG performance.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H2cGreen technological innovation mediates the relationship between digital transformation and corporate ESG performance.

2.5 Market concentration as a moderation mechanism: the extended Porter Hypothesis

Corresponding to RQ4, this subsection examines market concentration as a boundary condition that may strengthen or weaken the ESG-enhancing effect of digital transformation.

The Porter Hypothesis provides a useful theoretical basis for understanding how market structure may shape the environmental consequences of digital transformation. Porter and Linde (1995) argue that properly designed environmental pressures may stimulate innovation and generate innovation compensation effects. Zhang et al. (2024) find that in the context of digital transformation, market structure may influence whether firms allocate digital efficiency gains to short-term price competition or to long-term environmental investment.

Market concentration may have two competing effects on the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance. On the one hand, higher market concentration may reduce competitive pressure and generate a monopoly complacency effect. Firms with strong market power may face weaker external pressure to innovate, improve efficiency, or upgrade environmental practices. From this perspective, higher HHI may weaken firms’ incentives to transform digital capabilities into green innovation and environmental improvement (Giglio et al., 2025).

On the other hand, higher market concentration may create a resource slack and appropriability effect. Firms in more concentrated markets usually have stronger market power, more stable cash flows, greater strategic discretion, and a stronger ability to appropriate returns from long-term investments. These conditions are particularly important in the context of digital transformation because digital technologies often require complementary investments in data infrastructure, organizational restructuring, environmental management systems, and green R&D. Firms operating in highly competitive markets may use digital technologies mainly to reduce costs, improve operational efficiency, and defend market share. By contrast, firms in more concentrated markets may be better able to allocate digital efficiency gains toward environmental governance, green technological innovation, and climate-related investments (Sun et al., 2024).

In the context of Chinese A-share listed firms, this study expects the resource slack and appropriability effect to dominate the monopoly complacency effect. This expectation can be understood by extending the Porter Hypothesis from a regulation–innovation relationship to a market-structure–capability relationship. The Porter Hypothesis emphasizes that innovation compensation effects depend on whether firms have sufficient incentives and capabilities to transform environmental pressure into innovation and performance improvement. Market concentration shapes this transformation process by affecting firms’ resource slack, strategic discretion, competitive pressure, and ability to appropriate returns from long-term investments (Wang J. et al., 2023).

From the NRBV perspective, transforming digital capabilities into ESG performance requires complementary investments in environmental monitoring systems, green R&D, cleaner production processes, supply-chain traceability, and sustainability governance routines. These investments are costly, uncertain, and often associated with delayed returns. Firms in more concentrated industries may have more stable cash flows, stronger resource endowments, and greater bargaining power, which enable them to sustain long-term digital and green investments and appropriate the resulting benefits.

Stakeholder Theory further suggests that firms in concentrated industries may face greater visibility and stronger legitimacy pressure. Dominant firms are more visible to regulators, investors, customers, media, and local communities. As a result, they may have stronger incentives to use digital technologies to improve ESG disclosure, environmental governance, and stakeholder responsiveness. Therefore, although higher market concentration may weaken innovation incentives through monopoly complacency, this study expects the resource slack, appropriability, and visibility effects to dominate. Accordingly, market concentration is expected to amplify the ESG benefits of digital transformation.

Based on the above analysis, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H3Market concentration positively moderates the relationship between digital transformation and corporate ESG performance, such that the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance is stronger in more concentrated markets.

Based on the above research hypotheses and theoretical framework integrating the Natural Resource-Based View, Stakeholder Theory, and the Porter Hypothesis, Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework through which digital transformation influences corporate ESG performance.

3 Research design

3.1 Sample selection and data sources

This study uses panel data for Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2023. Financial data and corporate governance variables are obtained from the China Stock Market and Accounting Research (CSMAR) database, while ESG performance is measured using Huazheng ESG ratings. The 2009–2023 sample period covers several important policy and economic events, including the Paris Agreement in 2015, the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the launch of China’s national carbon emissions trading market in 2021, and the implementation of the 14th Five-Year Plan for the Digital Economy in 2022. This broad sample period allows the analysis to capture substantial variation in firms’ digitalization and ESG practices over time. We exclude observations with missing key variables, firms in the financial sector, and observations with evident data anomalies. The final sample consists of 32,609 firm-year observations. The representativeness of the sample is supported in three respects. First, the sample covers all non-financial A-share listed firms with available data during 2009–2023, rather than focusing on a single industry, region, or ownership type. Second, the sample includes firms from major sectors of China’s real economy, including manufacturing, mining, utilities, construction, transportation, information technology, real estate, wholesale and retail trade, and other services. Third, the industry distribution reported in Appendix Table A1 shows that the sample reflects the sectoral structure of China’s non-financial listed firms, with manufacturing firms accounting for the largest share while other industries remain meaningfully represented. Therefore, the sample is broadly representative of Chinese non-financial A-share listed firms, although the findings should not be generalized directly to unlisted firms or financial institutions. To reduce the influence of extreme values, all continuous variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

Industry fixed effects are not separately included in the baseline models because firm fixed effects absorb all time-invariant firm characteristics, including each firm’s industry affiliation. We do not include industry-year fixed effects because doing so would absorb the industry-year-level HHI variable, which is central to the moderation analysis. In addition, year fixed effects control for common macroeconomic and policy shocks. To examine the role of time-varying industry-level market structure, we calculate the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index at the industry-year level and introduce it in the moderation model. The industry composition of the sample is reported in Appendix Table A1.

3.2 Variable Selection

3.2.1 Dependent variable

The dependent variable in this study is corporate ESG performance (ESG), measured by Huazheng ESG ratings. Huazheng ESG ratings provide a comprehensive evaluation of listed firms’ environmental, social, and governance performance. Compared with single-dimensional environmental indicators, comprehensive ESG ratings capture firms’ broader sustainability performance, including environmental responsibility, social accountability, governance quality, information disclosure, and stakeholder responsiveness. Following prior studies, this study converts the Huazheng ESG rating categories into a numerical scale from one to 9, with higher values indicating better ESG performance. In the sample, the observed values range from 1 to 8, indicating that no firm received the highest rating during the sample period.

Huazheng ESG ratings are widely used in studies of Chinese listed firms because they provide broad coverage of A-share companies and are updated consistently over time. Nevertheless, ESG ratings may vary across providers due to differences in evaluation criteria and weighting schemes. Therefore, the use of a single ESG rating provider is acknowledged as a limitation.

3.2.2 Independent variable

The independent variable is corporate digital transformation (Dig). Conceptually, this study treats digital transformation as a dynamic green digital capability rather than the simple adoption of isolated digital technologies. This capability reflects firms’ ability to use digital technologies and data resources to sense environmental and stakeholder demands, process sustainability-related information, coordinate internal and external resources, and reconfigure organizational routines for ESG improvement.

Empirically, following Wu et al. (2021),digital transformation is proxied by the frequency of digital-related keywords in firms’ annual reports. This text-based measure captures the extent to which firms disclose and emphasize digital transformation activities. Although it may not fully measure the depth and quality of actual digital implementation, it provides a consistent firm-year proxy for firms’ digital transformation orientation and digital capability development.

3.2.3 Mediating variable

The mediating variable is green technological innovation (Greenco). Following Tao et al. (2021) findings. it is measured by the number of green patent applications. Green patent applications capture firms’ innovation output in green products, clean production processes, pollution control, energy conservation, and resource recycling. Following prior research, patent applications are used rather than granted patents because applications can reflect firms’ green innovation activities more timely and are less affected by approval lags.

It should be noted that green technological innovation mainly captures the environmental innovation channel. Because ESG performance is a comprehensive construct that includes environmental, social, governance, and disclosure-related dimensions, green technological innovation is expected to be one mediating mechanism rather than the only mechanism linking digital transformation to ESG performance.

3.2.4 Moderating variable

Market concentration (HHI) serves as the moderating variable. It is measured using the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index. For each industry-year, HHI is calculated as the sum of squared market shares of all firms in the industry. A higher HHI indicates a more concentrated market structure. This study uses HHI to examine whether market concentration conditions the effect of digital transformation on ESG performance.

3.2.5 Control variables

Drawing on existing research literature, this study employs the following variables as controls: Fixed Assets Ratio (FIXED), Cash Assets Ratio (Cashflow), Revenue Growth Rate (Growth), Debt-to-Asset Ratio (Lev), Book-to-Market Ratio (BM), Independent Director Ratio (Indep), Return on Assets (ROA), Largest Shareholder Ownership (Top1), and Management Shareholding (Mshare). All models include firm fixed effects to control for time-invariant firm characteristics and year fixed effects to control for common temporal shocks affecting all firms.

3.3 Model construction

Based on the research content, the empirical analysis models are constructed as follows:

Model One: Baseline Regression Modelwhere i and t denote company i in year t; represents the intercept; indicates the coefficient for the main independent variable, digital transformation; represents coefficients for control variables; signifies the individual (firm) fixed effect controlling for time-invariant firm characteristics; denotes the time (year) fixed effect controlling for common temporal shocks; and represents the random error term. ESG represents ESG performance measured through Huazheng ESG ratings; Dig represents the digital transformation level. Note that the baseline model tests the total effect of digital transformation on ESG performance without including the mediator (Greenco) or moderator (HHI), following the first step of Baron and Kenny’s (1986) mediation framework.

Model Two: Mediation Effect Model

In the mediation effect model, Equation 2 assesses whether digital transformation (Dig) significantly affects the mediating variable green technological innovation (Greenco). Equation 3 simultaneously includes both the independent variable (Dig) and mediating variable (Greenco) to examine whether green technological innovation mediates the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance. Following Baron and Kenny (1986) mediation testing procedure, mediation is established when: (1) Dig significantly affects ESG in Equation 1; (2) Dig significantly affects Greenco in Equation 2; and (3) when both Dig and Greenco are included in Equation 3, Greenco significantly affects ESG. If the coefficient of Dig remains significant after including Greenco, the results would indicate partial mediation; if the coefficient of Dig becomes insignificant, the results would indicate full mediation.

Equation 2 tests H2a by examining whether digital transformation promotes green technological innovation. Equation 3 tests H2b by examining whether green technological innovation is positively associated with ESG performance after controlling for digital transformation. H2c is supported if digital transformation significantly affects green technological innovation in Equation 2, green technological innovation significantly affects ESG performance in Equation 3, and the indirect effect of digital transformation on ESG performance through green technological innovation is statistically significant.

Model Three: The moderating effect of market concentration is tested using Equation 4.where represents the interaction term between digital transformation and market concentration. Following standard practice to reduce multicollinearity, both variables are mean-centered before creating the interaction term. A positive and significant coefficient on indicates that market concentration strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, which is consistent with H3 and the extended Porter Hypothesis, suggesting that concentrated market structures provide firms with resource slack to channel digital efficiency gains toward environmental improvements.

To keep the mediation analysis conceptually distinct from the moderation analysis, the mediation regressions focus on the indirect pathway through green technological innovation. The moderating role of market concentration is examined separately in the interaction model. The mediation and moderation analyses are estimated separately to maintain conceptual clarity: the mediation models focus on the indirect pathway through green technological innovation, whereas the moderation model examines whether market concentration conditions the digital transformation–ESG relationship.

The empirical analysis proceeds in three steps. First, the baseline model estimates the total effect of digital transformation on ESG performance without including the mediating or moderating variables. Second, the mediation models examine whether green technological innovation transmits the effect of digital transformation to ESG performance. Third, the moderation model introduces the interaction term between digital transformation and market concentration to test whether market concentration conditions the digital transformation–ESG relationship. This stepwise design ensures that the direct effect, mediation mechanism, and moderation mechanism are examined separately and interpreted consistently.

The correlations related to green technological innovation are also consistent with the proposed mediation mechanism. Green technological innovation is positively correlated with ESG performance (r = 0.112,p < 0.001), and digital transformation is positively correlated with green technological innovation (r = 0.030,p < 0.001). These results provide initial support for the argument that digital transformation may improve ESG performance partly by promoting green technological innovation.

Market concentration is negatively correlated with ESG performance (r = −0.043,p < 0.001), digital transformation (r = −0.029,p < 0.001), and green technological innovation (r = −0.012,p < 0.01). However, these pairwise correlations only reflect unconditional associations and do not directly test the moderating effect of market concentration. Hypothesis three concerns whether market concentration strengthens the marginal effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, which is examined through the interaction term between digital transformation and HHI in the regression analysis.

In addition, most correlations among the explanatory and control variables are relatively small. The largest absolute correlations are observed between FIXED and Cashflow (r = −0.295,p < 0.001), and between Lev and ROA (r = −0.298,p < 0.001), both of which are far below the commonly used threshold of 0.7. Therefore, the correlation results suggest that severe multicollinearity is unlikely to be a major concern. This issue is further examined using variance inflation factors in the following section.

4.3 Multicollinearity analysis

Before conducting the regression analysis, this study further examines potential multicollinearity among the explanatory variables using variance inflation factors (VIFs). As shown in Table 3, all VIF values are close to 1. The largest VIF is 1.194 for Cashflow, followed by 1.157 for FIXED and 1.156 for Lev. The mean VIF is 1.078. Since all VIF values are substantially below the conventional threshold of 10 and the more conservative threshold of 5, multicollinearity is unlikely to be a serious concern in the empirical models. These results support the reliability of the subsequent regression analysis.

4.5 Mediation effect analysis

This section addresses RQ2 and RQ3 by testing H2a, H2b, and H2c. Specifically, it first examines whether digital transformation promotes green technological innovation, then examines whether green technological innovation improves ESG performance, and finally evaluates whether green technological innovation mediates the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance.

Column (1) tests H2a by using Greenco as the dependent variable. The coefficient of Dig is positive and statistically significant, indicating that digital transformation promotes green technological innovation. This finding supports H2a.

Column (2) tests H2b by using ESG as the dependent variable and including both Dig and Greenco. The coefficient of Greenco is positive and statistically significant, suggesting that green technological innovation improves corporate ESG performance. This finding supports H2b. The coefficient of Dig remains positive and statistically significant after Greenco is included, indicating that green technological innovation only partially mediates the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance rather than fully mediating it.

The bootstrap results in Table 6 further test H2c. This approach is consistent with established mediation-effect testing procedures (Wen and Ye, 2014). The estimated indirect effect is positive and statistically significant, and the confidence interval excludes zero. Therefore, H2c is supported. However, the indirect effect accounts for only approximately 3.33% of the total effect, suggesting that green technological innovation is a statistically significant but economically modest channel.

The mediation evidence should be interpreted as partial mediation rather than full mediation. Since the direct effect of digital transformation remains statistically significant after green technological innovation is included, green technological innovation does not fully explain the digital transformation–ESG relationship. This result is consistent with the multidimensional nature of ESG performance. While green technological innovation mainly captures the environmental innovation channel, ESG ratings also reflect social responsibility, governance quality, disclosure transparency, and stakeholder responsiveness. Therefore, green technological innovation represents one important but non-exclusive mechanism through which digital transformation improves ESG performance.

4.6 Moderation effect analysis

This section addresses RQ4 and tests H3 by examining whether market concentration moderates the relationship between digital transformation and corporate ESG performance. HHI is employed as the moderator, ESG as the dependent variable, and Dig as the core explanatory variable.

The regression results are reported in Table 7. The coefficient of Dig_cent is significantly positive (β = 0.0029722, t = 10.28, p < 0.001), suggesting that digital transformation significantly improves corporate ESG performance. The coefficient of HHI_cent is also significantly positive (β = 0.1620039, t = 4.21, p < 0.001), indicating that market concentration is positively associated with ESG performance. Most importantly, the interaction term between digital transformation and market concentration is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.0091719, t = 4.95, p < 0.001). This finding provides evidence that market concentration positively moderates the effect of digital transformation on ESG performance. In other words, the ESG-enhancing effect of digital transformation becomes stronger as market concentration increases.

To provide a more intuitive interpretation, Figure 2 presents the simple slopes of digital transformation at low, medium, and high levels of HHI, defined as the mean minus one standard deviation, the mean, and the mean plus one standard deviation, respectively. The results show that the slope of Dig is substantially steeper under high HHI than under low HHI. This visual evidence is consistent with the regression results in Table 7 and confirms that the positive relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance is stronger in more concentrated markets.

FIGURE 2

Overall, the results support Hypothesis 3. The positive coefficient of the interaction term suggests that the resource slack and appropriability effect dominates the monopoly complacency effect in this setting. Although higher market concentration may reduce competitive pressure and weaken firms’ incentives to improve ESG practices, the empirical evidence indicates that, among Chinese A-share listed firms, firms in more concentrated industries are better able to convert digital capabilities into ESG performance improvements. This may be because these firms possess greater market power, more stable cash flows, stronger resource availability, and greater strategic flexibility. These advantages allow them to allocate the efficiency gains generated by digital transformation toward ESG governance, green innovation, environmental disclosure, and broader sustainability management. Conversely, firms in highly competitive markets may be more likely to use digital technologies primarily for cost reduction and short-term survival, thereby weakening the transformation of digital capabilities into ESG performance.

Although the unconditional correlation between HHI and ESG is negative, the fixed-effects regression coefficient becomes positive after controlling for firm characteristics, year effects, and other covariates, indicating that the simple correlation should not be interpreted as the conditional effect of market concentration.

4.7 Robustness checks and endogeneity tests

To assess the robustness of the baseline findings and mitigate potential endogeneity concerns, this study conducts a set of additional tests. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, endogeneity analyses are incorporated into the broader robustness-check framework. Specifically, we first use robust standard errors and alternative sample-period specifications. We then conduct an instrumental-variable two-stage least squares estimation and a lagged independent variable test to address potential omitted-variable bias, reverse causality, simultaneity, and measurement-error concerns.

4.7.1 Robust standard errors and sample-period robustness

To further verify the reliability of the baseline results, this study performs three robustness tests. First, robust standard errors are applied to alleviate concerns regarding potential heteroskedasticity. Second, the 2020 observations are excluded to avoid the possible disturbance caused by the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic. Third, the sample is restricted to the pre-pandemic period from 2009 to 2019 to examine whether the main conclusion holds in a relatively stable economic environment.

The results are reported in Table 8. Column (1) shows the estimation results with robust standard errors. Column (2) presents the results after excluding the 2020 sample. Column (3) reports the results using only the pre-pandemic sample from 2009 to 2019. Across all three specifications, the coefficient of Dig remains positive and statistically significant. Specifically, the coefficient of Dig is 0.00230 in Column (1), 0.00224 in Column (2), and 0.00118 in Column (3), with corresponding t-statistics of 5.95, 7.64, and 2.39, respectively. These findings confirm that the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance is robust to alternative standard error treatment and sample-period adjustments.

4.7.2 Instrumental variable estimation

Although the baseline fixed-effects model controls for time-invariant firm heterogeneity and common year shocks, potential endogeneity concerns may still arise from omitted variables, reverse causality, simultaneity, and measurement error. As a first endogeneity-related robustness check, this study conducts an instrumental-variable two-stage least squares estimation. This approach is consistent with common panel-data and instrumental-variable estimation strategies used to address endogeneity concerns (Arellano and Bond, 1991; Blundell and Bond, 1998; Windmeijer, 2005). The IV-2SLS estimation results are reported in Table 9.

Endogeneity test using leave-one-out industry-year digital transformation as an instrument.

This table reports the IV-2SLS, estimation results. The instrumental variable is the leave-one-out industry-year average digital transformation level, calculated as the average digital transformation of all other firms in the same industry-year, excluding the focal firm. Column (1) presents the first-stage regression, where firm-level digital transformation is regressed on the instrumental variable. Column (2) presents the second-stage regression, where ESG, performance is regressed on the fitted value of digital transformation. Control variables, firm fixed effects, and year fixed effects are included. t-statistics are reported in parentheses. ***, **, and * indicate significance at the 0.1%, 1%, and 5% levels, respectively.

This study uses the leave-one-out industry-year average digital transformation level, denoted as IDig, as an instrumental variable for firm-level digital transformation. IDig is calculated as the average Dig of all other firms in the same industry-year, excluding the focal firm. The relevance condition is supported because firms in the same industry and year are exposed to similar technological environments and industry-level digital adoption trends. However, the exclusion restriction is more difficult to verify because industry-year digitalization may be correlated with unobserved industry-year ESG pressures, environmental regulation, or supply-chain requirements. Therefore, the IV analysis is used as supplementary evidence rather than as definitive causal identification.

Column (1) reports the first-stage regression results. The coefficient of IDig is positive and statistically significant, indicating that firms’ digital transformation is strongly associated with the leave-one-out industry-year digitalization trend. The first-stage F-statistic is well above the conventional threshold of 10, suggesting that weak-instrument concerns are unlikely.

Column (2) presents the second-stage regression results. The coefficient of the instrumented digital transformation variable remains positive and statistically significant (β = 0.002,t = 6.848,p < 0.001). This result provides supplementary evidence that the positive association between digital transformation and ESG performance remains after using a peer-based instrumental-variable specification. However, because the exclusion restriction of the instrument cannot be directly verified, the IV results should be interpreted cautiously and should not be viewed as definitive causal evidence.

4.7.3 Lagged independent variable test

To further mitigate potential reverse causality and simultaneity concerns, this study replaces the current value of digital transformation with its one-period lagged value, Digt−1. This approach helps reduce the possibility that current ESG performance simultaneously affects current digital transformation because current ESG performance is less likely to influence digital transformation decisions made in the previous period.

Table 10 reports the estimation results. The coefficient of Digt−1 is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.00207,t = 5.47,p < 0.001), indicating that past digital transformation is positively associated with current ESG performance. This finding is consistent with the baseline regression results and further alleviates concerns about reverse causality and simultaneity.

Endogeneity test—lagged independent variable.

This table reports the endogeneity test using the one-period lagged value of digital transformation. Column (1) presents the regression with control variables only, while Column (2) further includes the lagged digital transformation variable,Digt-1. Control variables, firm fixed effects, and year fixed effects are included but are not fully reported for brevity. t-statistics are reported in parentheses. R2 refers to the within-R2. ***, **, and * indicate significance at the 0.1%, 1%, and 5% levels, respectively.

Overall, the results of the IV-2SLS estimation and the lagged independent variable approach consistently show that digital transformation has a positive and statistically significant effect on ESG performance. These findings suggest that the baseline conclusion is not driven solely by observable time-invariant heterogeneity or simple reverse causality, although these tests do not fully eliminate all endogeneity concerns.

Although the instrumental variable approach helps mitigate endogeneity concerns, the exclusion restriction cannot be verified directly. Industry-level digitalization may be correlated with unobserved industry-level changes in regulation, supply-chain pressure, or ESG expectations. Therefore, the IV results should be interpreted as supplementary evidence rather than definitive causal identification. Future studies could use stronger instruments based on exogenous digital infrastructure shocks, city-level broadband penetration, or digital finance development.

4.8 Additional heterogeneity analyses

This section addresses RQ5 by examining whether the effect of digital transformation on ESG performance varies across regions, ownership types, and pollution-related industry groups. These analyses are exploratory extensions of the main hypotheses and help assess the generalizability of the baseline findings within the Chinese A-share listed-firm sample.

4.8.1 Regional heterogeneity

To examine whether the impact of digital transformation on ESG performance varies across regions, this study divides the sample into Eastern, Central, and Western regions. Regional differences in digital infrastructure, industrial structure, economic development, and policy support may influence the role of digital transformation in improving corporate ESG performance.

Table 11 presents the regional heterogeneity results. The coefficient of Dig is positive and statistically significant in all three regions. Specifically, the coefficient is 0.00254 in the Eastern region with a t-statistic of 8.19, 0.00310 in the Central region with a t-statistic of 3.30, and 0.00210 in the Western region with a t-statistic of 2.08. These findings indicate that digital transformation significantly promotes ESG performance across all regions, with the strongest effect observed in the Central region, followed by the Eastern region and the Western region.

Heterogeneity analysis by ownership type.

This table reports the ownership heterogeneity analysis. Column (1) presents the results for state-owned enterprises, and Column (2) presents the results for non-state-owned enterprises. The dependent variable is firms’ ESG, performance, and the key independent variable is digital transformation, measured by Dig. All regressions control for firm fixed effects and year fixed effects. The t-statistics reported in parentheses are based on standard errors clustered at the firm level. ***, **, and * indicate statistical significance at the 0.1%, 1%, and 5% levels, respectively.

A comparison of the estimated coefficients further shows that the coefficient of Dig is slightly larger for SOEs than for non-SOEs. One possible explanation is that SOEs generally bear stronger policy responsibilities and social obligations and are subject to closer government supervision and institutional constraints in terms of environmental protection, social responsibility, and corporate governance. Therefore, during the process of digital transformation, SOEs may be more likely to apply digital technologies to environmental information disclosure, resource allocation optimization, internal governance improvement, and social responsibility practices, thereby enhancing their ESG performance. In contrast, although non-SOEs can also improve ESG performance through digital transformation, their resource endowments, financing constraints, and external regulatory pressures may vary more substantially, which may weaken the ESG-enhancing effect of digital transformation.

Overall, the results in Table 12 suggest that digital transformation significantly promotes ESG performance in both SOEs and non-SOEs, with the effect appearing to be slightly more pronounced among SOEs. Nevertheless, since subsample regressions do not directly test whether the coefficient difference between groups is statistically significant, the comparison of coefficient magnitudes should be interpreted with caution and, where possible, supplemented by interaction-term tests.

High-polluting industries are identified according to the industry classification used in Chinese environmental regulation and prior studies.
